National Weather Service Burlington VT
304 PM EDT Tue Aug 25 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 303 PM EDT Tuesday...

No significant changes were made to the forecast with this package.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 303 PM EDT Tuesday...

1. Showers wind down this evening, with drier weather on 
Wednesday.

2. Another round of showers and thunderstorms on Thursday, with 
some storms possibly strong to locally severe. 

3. A tranquil period over the weekend will be followed by more 
shower and thunderstorm chances early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 303 PM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Scattered showers will continue to drift across the 
region this afternoon as the upper trough swings overhead. Activity 
will wane toward sunset with the loss of daytime heating. High 
pressure starts to nose into the area tonight and crosses on 
Wednesday, bringing a period of fair weather. After initial clearing 
this evening, clouds will likely increase overnight, particularly 
over the higher terrain, as moisture gets trapped under the 
inversion. Lows tonight will mainly be in the 50s, except in the 
usual sheltered valleys of the Adirondacks and Northeast Kingdom 
which could dip into the 40s. 

Wednesday will be a pleasant day under partly to mostly sunny skies. 
Winds will be light as we'll be under the influence of the ridge. 
Temperatures will top out in the mid 70s to low 80s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Precipitation chances will increase again Thursday into 
Friday as another upper trough pushes eastward across the Great 
Lakes and into the Northeast. Meanwhile, a weak surface low will 
slide across Ontario into Quebec, dragging a frontal boundary across 
the region in its wake. While moisture doesn't look particularly 
impressive, increasing instability ahead of the front and forcing 
from the approaching trough will allow for the development of 
showers Thursday afternoon. Shear of 30-35 kt will lend toward 
organization of storm cells, with some storms potentially becoming 
strong to locally severe. While areas just to our south seem the 
most favorable, SPC's Day 3 Marginal Risk of severe thunderstorms 
definitely seems reasonable, with strong winds and hail the main 
threats.  

Additional showers are expected on Friday as another shortwave 
rotates around the base of the upper trough, swinging another 
frontal boundary across our region. Limited instability will keep 
the threat of severe weather low, but still anticipate some rumbles 
of thunder, especially in central/southern VT where the front should 
come through during the mid-late afternoon. 

Both Thursday and Friday will feature highs in the mid 70s to mid 
80s, though much of northern NY will be cooler on Friday with the 
cold frontal passage earlier in the day there. Nights will remain 
comfortable with lows in the 50s to around 60F.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Another dry weekend with seasonable temperatures and low 
humidity is on track. Following the expected fair weather, a thermal 
ridge will translate eastward towards or into our region on Monday 
and will quickly be replaced by a trough. While a warming trend is 
the consensus for early next week, the ECMWF ensemble slightly 
favors a scenario where the ridge remains well to our west and 
temperatures are near to slightly below normal. In contrast, the 
latest AIGFS shows 850 mb anomalies reaching into the 90-97th 
percentile Monday afternoon with the ensemble mean in the 80-85th 
percentile, leading to well above normal temperatures. Statistical 
guidance generally supports temperatures just a bit above normal, 
with highs reaching the mid to upper 70s.

In association with seasonable warmth and increasing humidity, 
the most noteworthy part of the longer term pattern would be a 
risk of thunderstorms early next week. Some signals in the 
machine learning guidance and global ensemble clusters of 
CAPE/Shear suggest Vermont, and especially southern/western 
areas, may have favorable ingredients in place, but overall the 
risk currently looks more favorable south of our region. This 
thunderstorm potential is highly conditional on how Monday plays
out; with the passage of a cold front earlier in the day on 
Tuesday, there would be little or no activity that day. A later 
passage would support stronger variety storms on Tuesday, while 
Monday generally looks a bit more likely to see showers and 
thunderstorms generally. Large uncertainty keeps thunder 
probabilities rather low (mainly under 15%, lower Tuesday than 
Monday) but bears watching. At the least, this period looks 
unsettled with rain at some point rather likely. Rainfall 
probabilities of exceeding 1" are generally in the 15-30% range 
over the course of the two days, and 20-50% of exceeding 0.5".

&&

.AVIATION /19Z TUESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 18Z Wednesday...Aside from lingering MVFR ceilings at MSS,
VFR conditions will continue through at least 00Z at all terminals.
During the next six hours, brief intervals of MVFR conditions due to
a combination of visibility and ceilings will be possible associated
with scattered showers dotting the airspace. Radar trends put
showers within the vicinity but with low chance of a direct hit, as
they are rather small and mainly tracking south/west of some
terminals including RUT, PBG, BTV, and MSS. Lowest chances of
precipitation appears to be at MPV. Associated with these showers a
brief wind gust in the 15 to 20 knot range will be possible but
winds largely will remain light and variable through much of the
period.  Moderately high dew points today and some light
northwesterly flow through the overnight, along with any evening
showers, will support low cloud formation. It is a tricky
combination with regards to prediction of IFR conditions, with the
pattern favoring more MVFR ceilings rather than IFR unless fog
develops amidst patches of clear skies with the exception of the
higher elevation sites (SLK, MPV, EFK). Among these sites,
prevailing IFR conditions at MPV is most likely (greater than 70%)
during much of the 06Z to 12Z period. High pressure building in will
lead to gradual improvement/scattering of any remaining low ceilings
between 12Z and 18Z.
